name_native: ชาดำ / ชาไทย
origin_region: Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai highlands (Mae Salong, Mae Chan, Doi Wawee, Mae Taeng)
cultivar: Assamica-type bushes and semi-wild trees of the northern hills, plus some Taiwanese cultivars on the newer farms
processing: Mostly strong broken-leaf and CTC-style black tea for the Thai milk-tea trade; the commercial 'Thai tea' mixes add spices and colouring to the tea. A smaller amount of orthodox whole-leaf black tea is made on the Mae Salong and Mae Chan farms, withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried.
harvest_season: Picked through the year in the tropical hills, with the cool dry season (November to February) giving the best orthodox lots; the bulk tea is harvested whenever the bushes flush.
appearance_dry: Small, dark, broken leaf for the bulk tea; the commercial mixes are rust-orange from colouring. Orthodox lots are wiry black leaves with some golden tips.
appearance_liquor: Deep red-brown and strong; the coloured mixes brew an unmistakable bright orange. Orthodox lots are clear copper.
appearance_wet: Dark brown broken leaf; whole copper leaves in the orthodox lots.
taste_profile: The bulk tea is strong, malty and tannic, built to stand up to condensed milk and ice; the orthodox hill lots are softer, with malt, dried fruit and a honeyed, slightly earthy sweetness.

brewing.notes: For cha yen, brew much stronger (about 10 g per 300 ml, 5 minutes, or simmer briefly), strain, sweeten with sugar and condensed milk, pour over ice and top with evaporated milk. Orthodox hill lots can be brewed gongfu-style.

vintage_note: The milk-tea base is sold year-round by brand in bags and tins (the spiced, coloured mixes have no vintage and keep for a year or two); it is never sold by harvest. The small-farm orthodox black teas are sold as the current year's lot, vacuum-packed, and are best within a year or two of picking.
description:
Thailand's famous orange iced tea, cha yen, starts with black tea, and most of that tea is grown in the northern hills. The assamica-type bushes and semi-wild trees of Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai have been picked for centuries for miang, the fermented chewing tea, and in the twentieth century the same leaf was turned into strong black tea for the milk-tea trade. The commercial 'Thai tea' mixes that go into the drink add star anise, other spices and a food colouring that gives the brew its colour; the tea underneath is a robust broken-leaf black.

That bulk tea is designed to be brewed very strong, sweetened with sugar and condensed milk and poured over ice, and it is excellent at that job. Brewed plain, it is simply a big, tannic, malty black tea, not unlike a plain Assam. It is sold by brand rather than by garden or season, and the same leaf also goes into the less sweet 'cha dam yen' and the lime version.

The more interesting side is recent: the oolong farms around Mae Salong and Mae Chan now also make orthodox whole-leaf black tea, sometimes from the old assamica trees, sometimes from the Taiwanese cultivars they grow for oolong. These are softer teas, with malt, dried fruit and a honeyed, slightly earthy sweetness, and they can be brewed gongfu style. Thai shops often call them 'red tea', the Chinese way.

When buying, decide which you want. For cha yen, buy a Thai brand mix and follow the strong-brew-and-condensed-milk method; a 'natural' version without colouring will taste the same and look brown. For a tea to drink on its own, look for an orthodox black from a named northern farm with a harvest year. Imported Ceylon and Assam leaf also goes into some Thai mixes, so 'Thai tea' on the label is not a guarantee of Thai-grown leaf.

If you like the spiced side, make cha yen from a good plain Thai black with a star anise in the pot and skip the colouring; it is the same drink without the orange.
sources_note: The Wikipedia 'Thai tea' article is about the drink (cha yen) rather than the tea leaf; it is the closest umbrella. The claim that some commercial mixes use imported Ceylon/Assam leaf is based on ingredient lists and trade knowledge rather than a single source. Taste tag 'spicy' refers to the spiced commercial mixes.
